C005.subject: The growth trajectory of AI scaling trends
C005.object: the inability of current architectures to internalize compositional generalization from sparse training examples, independent of data distribution mismatch
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The growth trajectory of AI scaling trends the inability of current architectures to internalize compositional generalization from sparse training examples, independent of data distribution mismatch]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled synthetic benchmarks for compositional generalization (e.g., COGS, CFQ, or SCAN) with systematic variation in training example sparsity and distributional properties, tested on current large-scale transformer models — Directly tests whether architectures fail to internalize compositional rules from sparse examples when data distribution is controlled, isolating the hypothesized constraint from distribution mismatch.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of transformer attention mechanisms and their capacity for systematic compositionality, building on work by Lake & Baroni (2018), Hupkes et al. (2020), and recent mechanistic interpretability studies — Provides formal grounding for whether current architectures lack the inductive bias necessary for compositional generalization from sparse data, independent of distributional factors.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of scaling law studies (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) combined with negative results on novel reasoning benchmarks (e.g., BIG-Bench, ARC, GSM8K) since 2023, focusing on performance plateaus despite increased compute and data — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether observed scaling limitations align with the hypothesized compositional generalization failure, controlling for distribution mismatch via benchmark design.

scope.domain: large-scale language model performance on novel reasoning benchmarks

C006.subject: The growth trajectory of AI scaling trends
C006.object: the development of novel architectures and adaptive learning techniques that improve out-of-distribution reasoning
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The growth trajectory of AI scaling trends the development of novel architectures and adaptive learning techniques that improve out-of-distribution reasoning]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative evaluation of OOD reasoning performance across transformer-based models (e.g., GPT-4, Llama 3) and novel architecture variants (e.g., State Space Models, Mixture-of-Experts) on benchmarks like BIG-Bench Hard or MMLU under distribution shift conditions — Direct empirical measurement of whether novel architectures improve out-of-distribution (OOD) reasoning relative to standard scaling baselines, controlling for compute budget, would provide evidence for or against the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of scaling laws under architectural changes, e.g., extending Kaplan et al. (2020) or Hoffmann et al. (2022) to model the effect of adaptive learning techniques (like meta-learning or dynamic routing) on scaling exponents for OOD tasks — A formal theoretical framework predicting how novel architectures modify scaling trajectories would allow testing the hypothesis via derived predictions that can be compared with empirical scaling curves.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review of recent preprints (2024-2026) from major AI labs (Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta) reporting scaling experiments with novel architectures (e.g., Mamba, Hyena, or retrieval-augmented transformers) and their OOD reasoning performance — Aggregating documented results across labs can reveal whether there is a consistent trend of accelerated scaling due to architectural innovations, or whether gains are marginal or context-dependent, thereby confirming or refuting the hypothesis.

C007.subject: The growth trajectory of AI scaling trends
C007.object: architectural innovations that introduce sparse computation and modular specialization

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of computational complexity in modular vs. monolithic architectures, focusing on the trade-offs between sparsity-induced efficiency and routing overhead — Provides formal bounds on whether sparse computation can sustain or alter the scaling trajectory, helping to predict limits of reversal beyond empirical observations.

C008.subject: The growth trajectory of AI scaling trends
C008.object: emergent capabilities in reasoning and generalization as model size increases
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: The growth trajectory of AI scaling trends emergent capabilities in reasoning and generalization as model size increases]

[PATH:empirical] Systematic re-analysis of scaling laws across models of varying sizes (e.g., 7B, 13B, 70B, 175B) on reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K, MATH, and BIG-Bench, controlling for training compute and data quality. — Directly tests whether reasoning and generalization capabilities emerge discontinuously beyond certain model scales, which would confirm or refute the hypothesis that such emergence enhances the growth trajectory beyond simple scaling trends.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework from mechanistic interpretability (e.g., induction heads, circuit analysis) that predicts conditions under which compositional reasoning should appear, compared to observed scaling behavior. — Provides causal explanations for emergent reasoning, allowing predictions that can be empirically validated; if theory predicts emergence at specific scales but data shows monotonic improvement, the hypothesis would be weakened.
